Chief Executive’s Foreword 
 
I hope you all had a very enjoyable Halloween break. 
This year, we were very pleased that Fingal was 
chosen as a hub for ‘Ireland, Home of Halloween’ – 
The strategy, which was developed collaboratively by 
Fáilte Ireland, Tourism Ireland, and Tourism Northern 
Ireland, seeks to create a link with our Halloween 
festivities and our ancient history and culture and the 
marking of Samhain, which traditionally meant the 
end of the harvest season and the beginning of 
winter. The Wonderful family friendly events which 
took place complemented the already stellar 
Halloween 
programme 
planned 
and 
ensured 
enjoyment for all not just on Halloween night itself 
but throughout the month of October. In addition to 
the incredible programme of safe, accessible and fun 
events which took place across Fingal in celebration 
of the season of Samhain, three spectacular fireworks 
displays took place in Bremore Castle, Balbriggan, 
Swords 
Town 
Park 
and 
Millennium 
Park, 
Blanchardstown. Thousands of spectators came out 
to enjoy the music and soak up the atmosphere 
before the night sky was illuminated with stunning 
fireworks displays. I have received many messages of 
thanks from people who thoroughly enjoyed the 
various Halloween events showcased in Fingal and I 
wish to thank everyone involved in the planning and 
staging of these events.

The SuperValu TidyTowns competition has been 
promoting civic pride, environmental awareness, and 
community involvement across Ireland since 1958. 
This year, over 900 towns entered the competition 
demonstrating the huge interest from community 
groups in showcasing their localities and encouraging 
people to get involved in their areas. There was great 
celebration when the results were released with 
towns in Fingal scoring very highly in this year’s 
competition. All the dedicated committees across the 
county received higher scores than in 2024. Skerries 
was awarded County Second and a Gold Medal, while 
Malahide was awarded County Third and a Gold 
Medal. Swords was also awarded a Gold Medal, while 
Lusk, Rush and Balbriggan all received Bronze 
medals. There was also success for Clonsilla, with the 
group receiving an Endeavour Award for the biggest 
improvement by an entrant in the county from the 
previous year, improving by 32 points on 2024. Howth 
TidyTowns was highly commended in the EPA Circular 
Economy award, with Malahide receiving second 
prize in this category. Mayor of Fingal Cllr Tom 
O’Leary offered his congratulations to all the 
TidyTowns winners on a fantastic result. On behalf of 
myself and the Executive Management Team I would 
like to echo the Mayor’s sentiments in acknowledging 
the stellar work carried out by TidyTowns groups 
across Fingal each week. For many years our 
Operations Department has worked collaboratively 
with TidyTowns groups and in Fingal County Council, 
we have the highest regard for the volunteers and the 
tireless work they carry out in their communities. 
Fingal’s County Architect Fionnuala May has been 
elected as President of the Royal Institute of the 
Architects of Ireland (RIAI) for 2026-2027 after being 
nominated for the position by the RIAI Council. She is 
the 66th person to hold the position since it was first 
established in 1839 and the fifth woman. Fionnuala 
joined Fingal County Council in 1994 and, as the head 
of the Architect’s Department, she has been involved 
extensively in projects in the areas of housing, public 
buildings, corporate offices and heritage buildings. 
Fionnuala brings to the role her wealth of experience 
and knowledge and it is a testament to her years of 
dedicated work that she has been elected by her 
peers. I know you will join me in warmly 
congratulating Fionnuala and wish her all the very 
best as she begins her term as President of the RIAI. 
 
Best wishes,  
AnnMarie Farrelly

Arts Act Grant Scheme 
 
 
 
Fingal Arts Office announced that applications for 
the Arts Act Grant Scheme 2026 opened on 
Thursday 10th October 2025 and will close on 
Friday 5th December 2025 at 4.00pm. 
 
The scheme is designed to support individual 
artists, community groups, and arts organisations 
engaged in arts and cultural activities in Fingal. 
Grants are awarded under the Arts Act 2003 and 
reflect its objectives of promoting the arts, 
increasing access to the arts, and supporting 
cultural development across the county. 
 
This scheme welcomes applications across a wide 
range of artforms, including theatre, literature, 
music, dance, opera, film, circus, architecture, 
visual arts and multi-disciplinary projects, events 
and festivals.

The Seamus Ennis Arts Centre 
 
October was a busy month for The Seamus Ennis 
Arts Centre with our ongoing exhibition, music and 
art classes, singing sessions and slow sessions, 
plus special events for the Fingal Home of 
Halloween month. 
 
Home of Halloween 
 
The Home of Halloween programme kicked off on 
October 5th with the Harvest Food Fair, featuring 
22 stands selling a variety of local fruit and veg, 
homemade bakes, artisan breads, farmhouse 
cheeses, jams and chutneys, kombucha, cordials, 
Italian products, chocolates, locally roasted coffee 
and much more. In addition we hosted a Herbs, 
Hexes and Halloween workshop for adults with 
Denise Dunne exploring Samhain traditions and 
Irish Herbal Lore with 24 attendees (sold out), and 
four sold out children’s cookery classes in 
conjunction with the Fingal Food Circle (80 
attendees). Overall we had over 1100 attendees on 
the day. 
 
 
 
 
Over the midterm we hosted a variety of special 
Home of Halloween children’s craft workshops 
(all sold out – 72 participants in total), with animal 
sculpture in clay, fused glass creations, an owl log 
workshop and a dreamcatcher workshop. Our 
children’s programme ended with the magical film, 
The Book of Kells on October 30.

Rounding out the HoH month was a talk focused 
on Fourknocks, our local passage tomb entitled 
Death in the Neolithic on October 24 – sold out 
(92 attendees), an Irish language horror film, An 
Taibhse (The Ghost) on October 30, and finishing 
up with a talk and whiskey tasting night Uisce 
Beatha – Monks, Moonshine and Mythical 
Mashbills with Rosi Goswell and Garry Quinn.

Murray (48 attendees) and on October 17, Ye

Within our traditional music programme, we had

each week. We had 8 people for The Pop Up 
Gaeltacht join us before the Singing Sessions (17 
in person, 17 online) and the Slow Sessions (16 in 
person, 29 online) continued to support both 
learners and those more experienced in engaging 
with the Irish language, instruments and song.

Default Speed Limits Update 
Regarding the 30kph in built up & urban areas, the 
Department 
of 
Transport 
previously 
communicated to Councils that we were to 
proceed with the review and implementation of 
urban speed limits by special speed limit bye-laws 
rather than a change in the default speed limit .   
In order to undertake the process of setting special 
speed limits in built up & urban areas, the 
Guidelines for Setting and Managing Speed Limits 
in Ireland were being revised.  All LA’s have been 
eagerly awaiting their publication.  They have just 
been issued to Councils on the 16/10/2025 via a 
new Circular.  The Circular has directed the LA’s to 
commence the process of reviewing existing speed 
limits on roads in built-up and urban areas & to set 
speed limits in accordance with the newly 
published technical Guidelines. LA’s will, where 
appropriate, introduce 30 km/h speed limits, such 
as on roads in the urban/built up areas in cities, 
towns & villages. 
The direction by the Minister is for local authorities 
to start this process with the objective of having 
the 30km/h speed limits in built-up and urban 
areas operational by 31st March 2027. 
Speed limit changes will be implemented by LAs, 
through the adoption of special speed limit bye-
laws, rather than by changing default limits. 
Making of bye-laws is a reserved function of local 
authorities elected members. 
 
Page 40 
Local authorities will hold a statutory public 
consultation process. Members of the public and 
stakeholders can make representations to LAs on 
any proposed speed limit changes, in line with the 
provisions of the Road Traffic Act 2004, as 
amended. 
Speed limits on roads in built-up and urban areas 
can only be changed where a majority of the 
elected members in a Local Authority vote to do so. 
In 2027, the speed limit changes will come into 
effect on the dates specified by each LA in their 
new bye-laws. Signs showing the new speed limit 
will be installed at appropriate locations, so that 
road users are aware of any change.

Preventing Homelessness, Notices to Quit and

Fingal County Council is aware that households in 
the Fingal area who may have received a notice to 
quit, which is also referred to as a notice of 
termination, from their landlord may be worried or 
unsure of what to do.  
 
Fingal County Council and the Dublin Regional 
Homeless Executive (DRHE) would like to advise 
anyone affected of the services that are available 
to them in these circumstances.  
 
We strongly encourage tenants residing in the 
Fingal area, who have been issued with a notice 
of termination, to contact Fingal County 
Council as soon as they receive a notice from 
their landlord. The contact details for Fingal 
County Council are provided at the bottom of 
this page.  
 
When the tenants contact Fingal County Council, staff in 
the Housing Department will take note of the 
termination date.  
 
The Council advises the tenant to refer the notice to 
Threshold, a service funded by the DRHE to provide a 
Tenancy Protection Service for private renters in the 
Dublin Region, including Fingal. Threshold can also be 
contacted directly on Freephone 1800 454 454 or via 
their website www.threshold.ie which contains more 
information and advice on the validity of your notice.  
 
The Council’s first response will be to try to prevent 
homelessness. This includes assessing the person’s 
position on the social housing list, providing advice on 
applying for Choice Based Lettings, and advising the 
person on the level of Housing Assistance Payment 
(HAP) they may be eligible to receive. 
  
Placement in emergency accommodation will be a last 
resort if no other alternative can be identified.
